title: Theorem
body_md:
{\em The morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra $\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} \longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$
is a localization by the pre-Bott classes $b_m$ for $m\geq 1$,
both in the $\infty$-category of ultra-commutative ring spectra,
and in the $\infty$-category of commutative global ring spectra.}
head: manual

title: Theorem
body_md:
{\em
    Let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
\item  The morphism of commutative $G$-ring spectra
  $\eta_G\colon\allowbreak \Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G\longrightarrow {\mathbf{KU}}_G$
    is a localization by the pre-Bott classes $b_{G,V}$
    for all unitary $G$-representations $V$,
    in the $\infty$-category of commutative $G$-ring spectra.
  \item For every $\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G$-module $M$ in ${\mathcal S} p_G^\wedge$,
    the morphism
    \[ \pi_\star^G(\eta_G\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G} M)\ : \  \pi_\star^G(M)  \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_\star^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G\wedge_{\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G} M) \]
    exhibits the target as a localization,
    in $RO(G)$-graded  $\pi_\star^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)$-modules,
    of the source by the set of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
   \item For every finite based $G$-CW-complex $A$, the morphism 
    \[  \eta^\star_G(A)\ : \  (\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)^\star(A)  \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathbf{KU}}_G^\star(A) \]
    exhibits the target as a localization,
    in $RO(G)$-graded  $(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G)^\star$-modules,
    of the source by the set of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
  \item The morphism of graded-commutative $RO(G)$-graded rings
    \[  \pi_\star^G(\eta_G)\ : \  \pi_\star^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}_G) \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_\star^G({\mathbf{KU}}_G) \]
    exhibits the target as an $RO(G)$-graded localization of the source by the set
    of pre-Bott classes of all unitary $G$-representations.
  \end{enumerate}
  }

title: Conventions
body_md:
We state our main results in higher categorical terms in the $\infty$-categories
of commutative or ultra-commutative global or $G$-equivariant ring spectra.
For definiteness, `$\infty$-category' shall in this paper mean `quasi-category',
and the more technical appendices draw heavily from Lurie's writings
\cite{lurie:htt, lurie:higher_algebra}. The exposition and proofs in the body
of the paper are largely agnostic to the particular model for higher categories,
and mostly use naturality and universal property arguments.
To get to $\infty$-categories, we use the 1-categorical models
for unstable and stable global homotopy theory provided in \cite{schwede:global}.
In other words: we model global spaces by orthogonal spaces,
and we model global spectra by orthogonal spectra,
relative to the respective classes of global equivalences.
In fact, I would not know how to construct the morphism
$\eta\colon \Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ with the full coherence that it supports
(i.e., as a morphism of Real-global ultra-commutative ring spectra) in model-independent terms.
head: manual

title: Definition
body_md:
We let $G$ be a compact Lie group, $E$ an orthogonal $G$-spectrum, 
  and $V$ an orthogonal $G$-representation.
  The $V$-graded $G$-equivariant homotopy group of $E$ is
  \[ \pi_V^G(E)\ = \ \operatorname{colim}_{U\in s({\mathcal U}_G)} [S^{U\oplus V},E(U)]^G_*\ .  \]
  The colimit is taken over the poset $s({\mathcal U}_G)$, under inclusion,
  of finite-dimensional $G$-subrepresentations of a complete $G$-universe ${\mathcal U}_G$,
  along stabilization maps much like in the integer-graded case.
head: environment
name: Representation-graded homotopy groups

label: def:RO-invertible
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:RO-invertible}
  Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, let $R$ be a homotopy $G$-ring spectrum,
  and let $V$ be a $G$-representation.
  A representation-graded homotopy class $v\in \pi_V^G(R)$
  is {\em invertible} if the morphism 
  $v^\flat \colon R\wedge S^V\longrightarrow R$  is an equivalence of $G$-spectra.
head: environment
name: Invertibility

label: rk:2invertibles
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk:2invertibles}
In Construction \ref{con:pi_star^G} we recall the $RO(G)$-graded
equivariant homotopy groups of a $G$-spectrum.
Invertibility in the sense of Definition \ref{def:RO-invertible}
is then essentially the same as invertibility in the $RO(G)$-graded homotopy ring $\pi_\star^G(R)$.
More precisely, a class $v\in \pi_V^G(R)$ is invertible in the representation-graded sense
just defined if and only if for some (hence any)
equivalence of $G$-spectra $\kappa\colon {\mathbb S}^{[V]}_G\sim \Sigma^\infty S^V$,
the class $\kappa^*(v)\in\pi_{[V]}^G(R)$ is a unit in the 
$RO(G)$-graded homotopy ring $\pi_\star^G(R)$.
The caveat is that while
the representation-graded homotopy group $\pi_V^G(R)$
is isomorphic to the $RO(G)$-graded homotopy group $\pi_{[V]}^G(R)$,
there is no preferred or `canonical' way to identify them.
head: environment

label: prop:invert_criterion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:invert_criterion}
  Let $V$ be a representation of a compact Lie group $G$,
  and let $R$ be a commutative homotopy $G$-ring spectrum.
  Then for a representation-graded homotopy class $v\in\pi_V^G(R)$,
  the following conditions are equivalent.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (a)]
  \item The class $v$ is invertible.
  \item There exists an element $u\in\pi_0^G(R\wedge S^V)$
    such that $v^\flat_*(u)=1$ in $\pi_0^G(R)$.
    \item For every closed subgroup $H$ of $G$, the class $\Phi^H(v)$
      is a homogeneous graded unit in the geometric fixed point ring $\Phi_*^H(R)$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(a)$\Longrightarrow$(b)
  Since the morphism $v^\flat\colon R\wedge S^V\longrightarrow R$ is an equivalence of $G$-spectra,
  the induced map of homotopy groups
  $v^\flat_*\colon\pi_0^G(R\wedge S^V)\longrightarrow\pi_0^G(R)$
  is bijective. In particular, the class $1\in \pi_0^G(R)$ has a preimage.

  (b)$\Longrightarrow$(c)
  We let $H$ be a closed subgroup of $G$.
  Applying the geometric fixed point homomorphism $\Phi^H\colon \pi_0^G(R)\longrightarrow\Phi^H_0(R)$
  to the relation $v^\flat_*(u)=1$ yields
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi^H_of_rel}
      \Phi^H_0(v^\flat)(\Phi^H(u))\ =\ \Phi^H(v^\flat_*(u))\ =\  \Phi^H(1)\ = \ 1   
  \end{equation}
   in $\Phi_0^H(R)$.
  A choice of orientation of $V^H$ induces a well-defined homotopy
  class of equivalence $S^l\sim S^{V^H}$, for $l=\dim(V^H)$. This, in turn, induces 
 isomorphisms
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:induced_fix_iso}
   \Phi^H_{m-l}(R) \
   \cong \ \Phi^H_m(R\wedge S^l) \
   \cong \ \Phi^H_m(R\wedge S^{V^H})\ \cong \ \Phi^H_m(R\wedge S^V)\ . 
 \end{equation}
 Moreover, composition of this isomorphism with the map
 $\Phi^H_m(v^\flat)\colon\Phi^H_m(R\wedge S^V)\longrightarrow \Phi^H_m(R)$ is multiplication
 by the element $\Phi^H(v)$.

 For $m=0$, we use this isomorphism to turn the class $\Phi^H(u)\in\Phi^H_0(R\wedge S^V)$
 into a class $\bar u\in\Phi_{-l}^H(R)$. The relation \eqref{eq:Phi^H_of_rel}
 then becomes the relation $\bar u\cdot\Phi^H(v)=1$.
 So the class $\Phi^H(v)$ has a left inverse.
 Since the homotopy $G$-ring spectrum $R$ is commutative,
 the graded ring $\Phi^H_*(R)$ is graded-commutative, so $\Phi^H(v)$ also
 has a right inverse, and is thus a graded unit.

  (c)$\Longrightarrow$(a) 
  For every closed subgroup $H$ of $G$ and choice of orientation of $V^H$,
  the composite of the isomorphism \eqref{eq:induced_fix_iso}
  with $\Phi^H_m(v^\flat)\colon \Phi^H_m(R\wedge S^V) \longrightarrow\Phi^H_m(R)$
  is multiplication by the class $\Phi^H(v)$.
  Because $\Phi^H(v)$ is a graded unit, multiplication by $\Phi^H(v)$ is bijective,
  hence so is the map $\Phi^H_m(v^\flat)$.
  So the morphism $v^\flat$ induces isomorphisms of geometric fixed point groups
  for all closed subgroups of $G$. Hence $v^\flat$ is an equivalence of $G$-spectra,
  which means that $v$ is invertible.
head: environment

label: prop:invert_inherit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:invert_inherit}
  Let $V$ be a representation of a compact Lie group $G$,
  let $R$ be a commutative homotopy $G$-ring spectrum,
  and let $v\in\pi_V^G(R)$ be a representation-graded homotopy class.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item If the class $v$ is invertible, then for every
    morphism $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ of commutative homotopy $G$-ring spectra,
    the class $i_*(v)\in\pi_V^G(S)$ is invertible.
  \item If the class $v$ is invertible, and $H$ is a closed subgroup of $G$,
    then the class $\operatorname{res}^G_H(v)\in \pi^H_V(R)$ is invertible.
  \item Let $w\in\pi_W^G(R)$ be another representation-graded homotopy class.
    Then the product $v\cdot w$ is invertible if and only if both $v$ and $w$ are invertible.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) For every closed subgroup $H$ of $G$, the morphism $i$ induces
  a homomorphism of graded rings $\Phi^H_*(i)\colon \Phi^H_*(R)\longrightarrow\Phi^H_*(S)$.
  Since $\Phi^H(v)$ is a graded unit by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion},
  the class 
  \[ \Phi^H_*(i)(\Phi^H(v)) \ = \ \Phi^H(i_*(v)) \]
  is a graded unit in the graded ring $\Phi^H_*(S)$.
  Since this holds for all closed subgroups $H$ of $G$,
  Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}
  shows that the class $i_*(v)$ is invertible. 

  (ii) The morphism $\operatorname{res}^G_H(v)^\flat\colon R\wedge S^V\longrightarrow R$
  is obtained from $v^\flat\colon R\wedge S^V\longrightarrow R$ by applying
  the restriction functor $\operatorname{res}^G_H\colon {\mathcal S} p_G\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p_H$.
  So if $v^\flat$ is an equivalence of $G$-spectra, then
  $\operatorname{res}^G_H(v)^\flat$ is an equivalence of $H$-spectra.

  (iii) We let $H$ be a closed subgroup of $G$.
  We choose orientations of $V^H$ and $W^H$, and then orient $(V\oplus W)^H$ by concatenating the
  chosen orientations.
  Then 
  \[ \Phi^H(v\cdot w)\ = \ \Phi^H(v)\cdot \Phi^H(w)  \]
  in $\Phi^H_{k+l}(R)$, where $k=\dim(V^H)$ and $l=\dim(W^H)$.
  So $\Phi^H(v\cdot w)$ is invertible in the graded ring $\Phi^H_*(R)$
  if and only if $\Phi^H(v)$ and $\Phi^H(w)$ are invertible.
  Since this holds for all closed subgroups $H$ of $G$,
  Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion} shows that
  $v\cdot w$ is invertible if and only if both $v$ and $w$ are invertible.
head: environment

label: eq:define_restriction
title: Construction
body_md:
We let $X$ be an orthogonal spectrum, and we let $\gamma\colon K\longrightarrow G$ be a continuous
  homomorphism of compact Lie groups. We define the {\em restriction homomorphism}
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_restriction}
    \gamma^*\ \colon\ \pi_V^G(X) \ \longrightarrow \ \pi^K_{\gamma^*(V)}(X)    
  \end{equation}
  by sending the class of a $G$-map $f\colon S^{U\oplus V}\longrightarrow X(U)$
  to the class of the $K$-map
  \[ S^{\gamma^*(U)\oplus \gamma^*(V)}\ = \
    \gamma^*(S^{U\oplus V})\ \longrightarrow \ \gamma^*(X(U)) \ = \ X(\gamma^*(U))\ . \]
  As in the special case $V=0$ in \cite[Construction 3.1.15]{schwede:global},
  we exploit here that elements of $\pi_{\gamma^*(V)}^K(X)$
  can be unambiguously represented by $K$-maps $S^{W\oplus\gamma^*(V)}\longrightarrow X(W)$
  for any $K$-representation $W$, not necessarily a subrepresentation of the chosen
  complete universe, see \cite[Construction 3.1.13]{schwede:global}.
  The restriction homomorphisms $\gamma^*$ are clearly contravariantly functorial
  for composition of group homomorphisms. When $\gamma$ is the inclusion of
  a subgroup $H\leq G$, then $\gamma^*$ specializes to the restriction homomorphism
  $\operatorname{res}^G_H$ considered above. The restriction homomorphism $\gamma^*$
  is a natural transformation between two functors from orthogonal spectra
  to abelian groups that both invert global equivalences.
  So $\gamma^*$ descends uniquely to a natural transformation
  between the descended functors from the $\infty$-category of global spectra
  to abelian groups; we abuse notation and denote the descended transformation
  by the same symbol.

  Whenever the continuous homomorphism $\gamma\colon K\longrightarrow G$ is surjective,
  the geometric fixed point homomorphism \eqref{eq:geom_fix_map}
  matches the restriction homomorphism \eqref{eq:define_restriction}
  with the inflation homomorphism \eqref{eq:define_inflation}
  on geometric fixed point homotopy groups, in the sense of the commutative square:
  \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\label{eq:infl_and_fix-ROG}
    \xymatrix{ \pi_V^G(X)\ar[r]^-{\gamma^*}\ar[d]_{\Phi^G} & \pi_{\gamma^*(V)}^K(X)\ar[d]^{\Phi^K}\\
      \Phi^G_k(X)\ar[r]_-{\gamma^*} &\Phi^K_k(X)    }      
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
  It is implicit that we use the same orientation for $V^G=(\gamma^*(V))^K$.
  The square commutes at the level of representatives by direct inspection.
head: environment
name: Restriction homomorphisms

label: prop:restriction_and_invert
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:restriction_and_invert}
  Let $\gamma\colon K\longrightarrow G$ be a continuous homomorphism of compact Lie groups.
  Let $R$ be a commutative global homotopy ring spectrum,
  and let $v\in \pi_V^G(R)$ be an invertible representation-graded homotopy class.
  Then the class $\gamma^*(v)$ in $\pi_{\gamma^*(V)}^K(R)$ is invertible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We let $L$ be a closed subgroup of $K$,
  and we set   $H=\gamma(L)$, a closed subgroup of $G$.
  The restriction of $\gamma$ to $L$ factors as a continuous epimorphism
  $\beta\colon L\longrightarrow H$,  followed by the inclusion of $H$ into $G$.
  Since $v$ is invertible, the class $\Phi^H(v)$ is a graded unit in the
  ring $\Phi^H_*(R)$, by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}.
  Since the inflation homomorphism $\beta^*\colon\Phi^H_*(R)\longrightarrow\Phi^L_*(R)$
  is a morphism of graded rings, the class
  \[ \beta^*(\Phi^H(v)) \ = \ \Phi^L(\beta^*(\operatorname{res}^G_H(v)))
    \ = \ \Phi^L(\gamma^*(v)) \]
  is invertible in the graded ring $\Phi^L_*(R)$.
  The first equation is the compatibility of inflation with geometric fixed point
  homomorphisms  \eqref{eq:infl_and_fix-ROG}, applied to $\beta\colon L\longrightarrow H$.
  Since this holds for all closed subgroups of $K$, the class
  $\gamma^*(v)$ is invertible by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}.
head: environment

label: def:global_loc
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:global_loc}
  Let $R$ be a commutative global ring spectrum.
  Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
  \item A morphism $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ of commutative global ring spectra
    {\em inverts ${\mathcal X}$} if for every
    element $v\in{\mathcal X}$ supported at $(G,V)$, the class $i_*(v)\in\pi_V^G(S)$
    is invertible in the sense of Definition \ref{def:RO-invertible}.
  \item 
  A {\em global localization by ${\mathcal X}$}
  is an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$ spanned by the
  ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Global localization

title: Remark
body_md:
The kind of localizations of ring spectra we study first arose in
non-equivariant homotopy theory. A special feature in that context is that
the localization of $R$ by a homotopy class $u\in\pi_n(R)$,
or more precisely its underlying spectrum, can always be calculated as the colimit,
classically modeled by a mapping telescope, of the sequence
\[ R \ \xrightarrow{\ \cdot u}\ R\wedge S^{-n}\ \xrightarrow{\ \cdot u}\ R\wedge S^{-2n}\xrightarrow{\ \cdot u}\ \dots \]
of iterations of the graded endomorphism of  $R$ that lifts multiplication by $u$,
compare \cite[Proposition 4.3.17]{lurie:ellipticII}.
Consequently, the topological localization always realizes the algebraic localization
on graded homotopy rings.

 
   \endgraf\endgroup\penalty-500\begingroup\parindent=0.0pt\clubpenalty=10000 
   \def\endgraf\endgroup{\endgraf\endgroup}\leavevmode
   \hangindent=2.4em\relax
   \hangafter=-2\relax
   \hbox to 0pt{\hss\relax
      \vbox to 0pt{\vskip-8pt\relax
        \hbox
          {\relax\dbend}
\vss}\kern.70em} We alert the reader that global localizations are {\em essentially never}
given by a sequential colimit over endomorphisms that resemble
`multiplication by the elements' to be inverted.
The issue is already present for localization at a class in
the equivariant homotopy rings of degree 0.
Much as in the $G$-equivariant context, the functor
$\pi_0^G\colon {\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ab}$ is represented by a global spectrum.
However, a key difference is that the representing object $\Sigma^\infty_+ B_{\operatorname{gl}}G$,
the unreduced suspension spectrum of the global classifying space of $G$,
is {\em not} invertible in the global stable homotopy category (unless the group is trivial).
In fact, the Picard group of the global stable homotopy category is isomorphic
to ${\mathbb Z}$, generated by the suspension of the global sphere spectrum,
see \cite[Theorem 4.5.5]{schwede:global}. In other words:
the only invertible global spectra are the `trivial spheres'. 
So if the class we wish to invert is supported at a nontrivial group,
there is not even any sequence of `graded endomorphisms' one might wish to take the colimit of.

The situation changes as soon as we fix a compact Lie group $G$
and pass to the underlying $G$-spectra.
As we show in Theorem \ref{thm:telescopic localization},
the spectrum ${\mathbf{KU}}_G$ is a `Bott-inverted telescopic localization' of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$,
i.e., a sequential colimit of copies of $\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}_G$ shifted by
the spheres of an exhaustive sequence of unitary representations,
along morphisms that represent multiplication by pre-Bott classes.

label: thm:loc_reg
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:loc_reg}
  Let ${\mathcal C}$ be a presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category.
  Let $\{\Phi^j\colon{\mathcal C}\longrightarrow{\mathcal S} p^\wedge\}_{j\in J}$ be a set
  of strong symmetric monoidal left adjoints.
  Let $R$ be a commutative algebra in ${\mathcal C}$,
  and let ${\mathcal W}$ be a full subcategory of $R\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal C})$.
  Let $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ be an object of ${\mathcal W}$.
  Suppose that the following conditions hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (a)]
  \item The functors $\{\Phi^j\}_{j\in J}$ are jointly conservative.
  \item  The $\infty$-category ${\mathcal W}$ is closed under postcomposition with morphisms in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal C})$.
  \item For every $j\in J$, the morphism of graded-commutative rings
    $\pi_*(\Phi^j(i))\colon \pi_*(\Phi^j(R))\longrightarrow \pi_*(\Phi^j(S))$
    is a localization by a set of homogeneous elements of the source,
    and for every object $f\colon R\longrightarrow P$ of ${\mathcal W}$,
    the morphism $\pi_*(\Phi^j(f))\colon\allowbreak \pi_*(\Phi^j(R))\longrightarrow \pi_*(\Phi^j(P))$
    factors through $\pi_*(\Phi^j(i))$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ is an initial object of ${\mathcal W}$.
head: environment
name: Localization recognition

title: Proof
body_md:
Throughout the proof we simplify notation by abbreviating $\pi_*(\Phi^j(R))$
  to $\Phi^j_*(R)$.
  In the examples where $\Phi^j$ is a geometric fixed point functor $\Phi^G$,
  the resulting notational ambiguity is resolved by Corollary \ref{cor:fix_ring_iso}.

  We let $f\colon R\longrightarrow P$ be any object of ${\mathcal W}$.
  Since ${\mathcal C}$ is presentably symmetric monoidal, the $\infty$-category $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal C})$
  has colimits.  We choose a pushout in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal C})$:
    \[  \xymatrix{ R\ar[r]^-i\ar[d]_f & S\ar[d]^g \\ 
P\ar[r]_-h & Q}       \]
  For every $j\in J$, the functor $\operatorname{CAlg}(\Phi^j)$ preserves colimits, so the square
  \[  \xymatrix@C=15mm{ \Phi^j(R)\ar[r]^-{\Phi^j(i)}\ar[d]_{\Phi^j(f)} & \Phi^j(S)\ar[d]^{\Phi^j(g)} \\
      \Phi^j(P)\ar[r]_-{\Phi^j(h)} & \Phi^j(Q)}       \]
  is a pushout of commutative ring spectra.
  By hypothesis, $\Phi_*^j(i)\colon \Phi_*^j(R)\longrightarrow \Phi_*^j(S)$
  is a localization of graded-commutative rings by some multiplicative
  subset $T$ of homogeneous elements of $\Phi_*^j(R)$.
  So the morphism of commutative ring spectra
  $\Phi^j(i)\colon \Phi^j(R)\longrightarrow \Phi^j(S)$ is also a localization by $T$,
  compare \cite[Proposition 4.3.17]{lurie:ellipticII}.
  Hence its cobase change
  $\Phi^j(h)\colon \Phi^j(P)\longrightarrow \Phi^j(Q)$
  is a localization by the subset
  $\Phi^j_*(f)(T)=\{\Phi^j_*(f)(x)\mid x\in T\}$ of $\Phi^j_*(P)$.
  Since $\Phi_*^j(i)$ inverts the elements of $T$,
  and since $\Phi_*^j(f)$ factors through $\Phi_*^j(i)$,
  also $\Phi_*^j(f)$ inverts the elements of $T$.
  So $\Phi^j(h)$ is a localization by a set of elements that are already invertible,
  and hence an equivalence.
  So $h$ is an equivalence by the joint conservativity of the functors $\Phi^j$.
  
  Since ${\mathcal W}$ is closed under postcomposition, $q=h f\simeq g i\colon R\longrightarrow Q$ lies in ${\mathcal W}$,
  and the pushout square exhibits $q$ as a coproduct of $f$ and $i$ in ${\mathcal W}$.
  As a coproduct, the map
  \[     {\mathcal W}(q,f) \ \longrightarrow \ {\mathcal W}(f,f)\times{\mathcal W}(i,f)\]
  is an equivalence of animae.
  Since $h$ is an equivalence, the first projection is an equivalence.
  And since ${\mathcal W}(f,f)$ is non-empty, the anima ${\mathcal W}(i,f)$ must be contractible.
  Since $f$ was an arbitrary object of ${\mathcal W}$, this proves that $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$
  is indeed an initial object of ${\mathcal W}$.

label: thm:fix_criterion
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fix_criterion}
  Let $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ be a morphism of commutative global ring spectra,
  and let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  Suppose that for every compact Lie group $K$, the morphism
  of $K$-geometric fixed point rings
  $\Phi^K_*(i)\colon \Phi^K_*(R)\longrightarrow \Phi^K_*(S)$
  is a localization by the set of classes $\Phi^K(\beta^*(x))$
  for all compact Lie groups $G$,
  all continuous homomorphisms $\beta\colon K\longrightarrow G$,
  and all classes $x\in{\mathcal X}$ supported at $G$.
  Then the morphism $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ is a global localization
  by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$.
head: environment
name: Geometric fixed point criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
We apply the localization recognition of Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg}
  to the presentably symmetric monoidal $\infty$-category ${\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}}$
  of global spectra, and to the family of geometric fixed point functors
  $\Phi^K\circ\operatorname{res}_K^\wedge\colon{\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}}\allowbreak\longrightarrow {\mathcal S} p^\wedge$,
  for $K$ ranging through representatives of all isomorphism classes of compact Lie groups.
  These functors are strong symmetric monoidal left adjoints, and jointly conservative.
  The full subcategory ${\mathcal W}$ of $R\backslash\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$
  is spanned by the ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms; it is closed under postcomposition
  by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_inherit} (i).
  The morphism $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ lies in ${\mathcal W}$: for every $v\in {\mathcal X}$
  supported at $G$, and all closed subgroups $K$ of $G$,
  the class $\Phi^K(i_*(v))=\Phi^K_*(i)(\Phi^K(\operatorname{res}^G_K(v)))$ is invertible by hypothesis,
  and so the class $i_*(v)$ is invertible by Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}.

  We claim that hypothesis (c) of Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg} holds for every compact Lie group $K$.
  Indeed, $\Phi^K_*(i)\colon \Phi^K_*(R)\longrightarrow \Phi^K_*(S)$
  is a localization by hypothesis, by the set of classes $\Phi^K(\beta^*(x))$
  as in the statement of the theorem.
  Moreover, if $f\colon R\longrightarrow P$ belongs to ${\mathcal W}$, then it inverts ${\mathcal X}$,
  and hence it inverts all the classes $\Phi^K(\beta^*(x))$ by
  Propositions  \ref{prop:invert_criterion} and \ref{prop:restriction_and_invert}.
  Since  $\Phi^K_*(i)\colon \Phi^K_*(R)\longrightarrow \Phi^K_*(S)$ is a localization by these
  classes, the morphism $\Phi^K_*(f)$ factors through $\Phi^K_*(i)$.
  So Theorem \ref{thm:loc_reg} applies and shows that $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$
  is a global localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$.
head: environment

title: Construction
body_md:
We let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  We recall that the wreath product $\Sigma_m\wr G$ with the symmetric group $\Sigma_m$ 
    is the semidirect product
  \[ \Sigma_m\wr G \ = \ \Sigma_m \ltimes G^m\] 
  formed with respect to the action of $\Sigma_m$ by permuting the
  factors of $G^m$. For every $G$-space $E$,
  the wreath product $\Sigma_m\wr G$ acts on the space $E^m$ by
  \[ (\sigma;\,g_1,\dots,g_m) \cdot (e_1,\dots, e_m) \ = \ 
    (g_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}e_{\sigma^{-1}(1)},\dots,g_{\sigma^{-1}(m)} e_{\sigma^{-1}(m)}) \ . \]
  For every $G$-representation $V$, this action even makes $V^m$ 
  a $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-representation.
  
  For a commutative orthogonal ring spectrum $R$,
  and for a $G$-representation $U$, we let
  \[ \mu_{U,\dots,U}\ : \
    R(U)\wedge\dots\wedge R(U) \ \longrightarrow \ R(U\oplus\dots\oplus U) \]
  denote the $(U,\dots,U)$-component of the iterated multiplication map of $R$.
  This map is $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-equivariant because the multiplication
  of $R$ is commutative.
  The $m$-th power operation
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_P^m}
    P^m \ : \ \pi_V^G(R)\ \longrightarrow \ \pi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}_{V^m}(R)    
  \end{equation}
  takes the class represented by a based $G$-map $f\colon S^{U\oplus V}\longrightarrow R(U)$
  to the class of the composite $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-map
  \begin{align*}
    S^{U^m\oplus V^m} \,  \cong \ S^{(U\oplus V)^m}\
    \xrightarrow{f^{\wedge m}}\ R(U)^{\wedge m} \  \xrightarrow{\mu_{U,\dots,U}} \ R(U^m) \ .
  \end{align*}
  The unnamed homeomorphism shuffles factors.
  Clearly, this power construction takes $G$-homotopic maps to 
  $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-homotopic maps. And if we stabilize $f$ by a $G$-representation
  $W$, then the composite gets stabilized by the
  $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-representation $W^m$. The upshot is thus a well-defined map
  \eqref{eq:define_P^m}.

  Much like for degree 0 homotopy classes in \cite[Remark 5.1.7]{schwede:global},
  the representation-graded power operations can be used to define
  representation-graded {\em norm maps}
  \[ N_H^G \ : \ \pi_W^H(R) \ \longrightarrow \ \pi_{\operatorname{ind}_H^G(W)}^G(R)\ ,\]
  for any finite index subgroup $H$ of $G$, where $W$ is an $H$-representation,
  and $\operatorname{ind}_H^G(W)$ is the induced $G$-representation.
  We refrain from spelling out the details because we will not use
  these norm maps in this paper.
head: environment
name: Representation-graded power operations

label: prop:invertibility_power
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:invertibility_power}
  Let $R$ be an ultra-commutative ring spectrum,
  and let $V$ be a representation of a compact Lie group $G$.
  Let $v\in \pi_V^G(R)$ be an invertible representation-graded homotopy class.
  Then for all $m\geq 1$, the class $P^m(v)$ in $\pi_{V^m}^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(R)$ is invertible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The morphism of $G$-spectra $v^\flat\colon R\wedge S^V\longrightarrow R$
  was defined in \eqref{eq:define_v_flat}.
  Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion} provides an element
  $u\in\pi_0^G(R\wedge S^V)$ such that $v^\flat_*(u)=1$ in $\pi_0^G(R)$.
  We suppose that $u$ is represented by the 
  continuous based $G$-map $f\colon S^U\longrightarrow R(U)\wedge S^V$.
  We define $P^m(u)\in \pi_0^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(R\wedge S^{V^m})$
  as the class represented by the $(\Sigma_m\wr G)$-map
  \[ 
    S^{U^m}\! =  (S^U)^{\wedge m} \xrightarrow{\ f^{\wedge m}} (R(U)\wedge S^V)^{\wedge m}
    \xrightarrow[\cong]{\text{shuffle}}  R(U)^{\wedge m}\wedge S^{V^m}
    \xrightarrow{\mu_{U,\dots,U}\wedge S^{V^m}}\ R(U^m)\wedge S^{V^m} .
  \]
  Then this class satisfies the relation
  \[  (P^m(v))^\flat_*(P^m(u)) \ = \ 1 \]
  in the group $\pi_0^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(R)$.
  So the class $P^m(u)$ witnesses criterion (b) of Proposition \ref{prop:invert_criterion}
  for the class $P^m(v)$, and thus $P^m(v)$ is invertible.
head: environment

label: def:ucom_loc
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ucom_loc}
  Let $R$ be an ultra-commutative ring spectrum, and
  let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  An {\em ultra-commutative localization by ${\mathcal X}$}
  is an initial object of the full subcategory of the
  slice category $R\backslash \operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$ spanned by the
  ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.
head: environment
name: Ultra-commutative localization

label: thm:UR2CR
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:UR2CR}
  Let $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ be a morphism of ultra-commutative ring spectra.
  Let ${\mathcal X}$ be a set of representation-graded equivariant homotopy classes of $R$.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item If the underlying morphism of commutative global ring spectra
    $u_{\operatorname{gl}} i\colon u_{\operatorname{gl}} R\longrightarrow u_{\operatorname{gl}} S$ is an epimorphism,
    then the following commutative square is a pushout in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$:
    \[  \xymatrix@C=13mm{ \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} R)\ar[r]^-{\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)}\ar[d]_{\epsilon_R} &
      \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} S)\ar[d]^{\epsilon_S}\\ R\ar[r]_-i & S}       \] 
\item Let $j\colon u_{\operatorname{gl}} R\longrightarrow T$ be a global localization by ${\mathcal X} $ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$,
  and let
  \[  \xymatrix@C=12mm{ \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} R)\ar[r]^-{\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(j)}\ar[d]_{\epsilon_R} &
        \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(T)\ar[d]^g \\ R\ar[r]_-i & S}       \]
    be a pushout in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
    Then $i\colon R\longrightarrow S$ is an ultra-commutative  lo\-cal\-iza\-tion
    by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
  \item If the underlying morphism of commutative global ring spectra
    $u_{\operatorname{gl}} i\colon u_{\operatorname{gl}} R\longrightarrow u_{\operatorname{gl}} S$ is a global localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$,
    then $i$ is an ultra-commutative localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:choose_po
title: Proof
body_md:
(i)
  We choose a pushout of $\epsilon_R$ and $\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$:
  \begin{equation}\begin{aligned}\label{eq:choose_po}
    \xymatrix@C=13mm{ \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} R)\ar[r]^-{\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)}\ar[d]_{\epsilon_R} &
      \lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} S)\ar[d]^g \\ R\ar[r]_-j & Q} 
    \end{aligned} \end{equation}
  Since $\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}$ is a left adjoint, it preserves pushouts and thus epimorphisms,
  so $\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)$ is an epimorphism in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
  Hence also its cobase change $j$ is an epimorphism.
  Since the functor $u_{\operatorname{gl}}$ is a left adjoint, it preserves pushouts and thus epimorphisms,
  so $u_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i))$ and $u_{\operatorname{gl}} j$ are epimorphisms in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p^\wedge_{\operatorname{gl}})$.

  The universal property of the pushout \eqref{eq:choose_po} provides a unique morphism
  $h\colon Q\longrightarrow S$ equipped with homotopies
  \[ h\circ j \ \sim \ i \text{\qquad and\qquad} h\circ g \ \sim \ \epsilon_S\ . \]
  Since $(u_{\operatorname{gl}} h)\circ (u_{\operatorname{gl}} j)\sim u_{\operatorname{gl}} i$ and both $u_{\operatorname{gl}} j$ and $u_{\operatorname{gl}} i$ are epimorphisms,
  also $u_{\operatorname{gl}} h\colon u_{\operatorname{gl}} Q\longrightarrow u_{\operatorname{gl}} S$ is an epimorphism.
  We write $\eta_P\colon P\longrightarrow u_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(P))$ for the unit of the adjunction.
  The sequence of homotopies
  \begin{align*} (u_{\operatorname{gl}} g)\circ\eta_{u_{\operatorname{gl}} S}\circ(u_{\operatorname{gl}} h)\circ (u_{\operatorname{gl}} j)\
    &\sim \ (u_{\operatorname{gl}} g)\circ\eta_{u_{\operatorname{gl}} S}\circ(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)\\
    &\sim \  (u_{\operatorname{gl}} g)\circ(u_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} i)))\circ\eta_{u_{\operatorname{gl}} R} \\
    &\sim \  (u_{\operatorname{gl}} j)\circ (u_{\operatorname{gl}}(\epsilon_R))\circ\eta_{u_{\operatorname{gl}} R}    \ \sim \ u_{\operatorname{gl}} j
  \end{align*}
  and the fact that $u_{\operatorname{gl}} j$ is an epimorphism show that
  the composite
  \[  u_{\operatorname{gl}} Q \xrightarrow{\ u_{\operatorname{gl}} h\ }\ u_{\operatorname{gl}} S \ \xrightarrow{\ \eta_{u_{\operatorname{gl}} S}\ }\ u_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} S))\
    \xrightarrow{u_{\operatorname{gl}} g}\ u_{\operatorname{gl}} Q \]
  is homotopic to the identity.
  So $u_{\operatorname{gl}} h$ is an epimorphism with a retraction, and thus an equivalence.
  Since $u_{\operatorname{gl}}$ is conservative, also $h\colon Q\longrightarrow S$ is an equivalence.
  Since the square \eqref{eq:choose_po} is a pushout, so is the square of the theorem.

  (ii)
  For every ultra-commutative ring spectrum $E$, the upper rectangle
  in the commutative diagram of animae
  \[  \xymatrix@C=12mm{
      \operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}(S,E)\ar[r]^-{i^*}\ar[d]_{g^*} & \operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}(R,E)\ar[d]^{\epsilon_R^*}
      \ar@<4ex>@/^3pc/[dd]^(.3){u_{\operatorname{gl}}}\\
       \operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(T),E)\ar[r]_-{\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(j)^*}\ar[d]_{\sim} &
       \operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}(\lambda_{\operatorname{gl}}(u_{\operatorname{gl}} R),E)\ar[d]^\sim \\
              \operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)(T,u_{\operatorname{gl}} E)\ar[r]_-{j^*}&
        \operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)(u_{\operatorname{gl}} R,u_{\operatorname{gl}} E) }       \]
   is a pullback, by the universal property of pushouts.
   The two lower vertical maps are the adjunction equivalences.
   So the outer rectangle is a pullback, too.
   Since $j$ is a localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$,
   the lower horizontal map is an equivalence onto the path components
   of ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms.
   A morphism $R\longrightarrow E$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$ is ${\mathcal X}$-inverting if and
   only if the underlying morphism in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$ is 
   ${\mathcal X}$-inverting.
   Hence the upper horizontal map is an equivalence onto the path components
   of ${\mathcal X}$-inverting morphisms. So $i$ has the defining property
   of an ultra-commutative localization by ${\mathcal X}$.

   (iii) Since localizations are epimorphisms, the square of part (i)
   is a pushout in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$.
   Since $u_{\operatorname{gl}} i\colon u_{\operatorname{gl}} R\longrightarrow u_{\operatorname{gl}} S$ is a global localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{CAlg}({\mathcal S} p_{\operatorname{gl}}^\wedge)$
   by hypothesis, 
   $i$ is an ultra-commutative localization by ${\mathcal X}$ in $\operatorname{URing}_{\operatorname{gl}}$ by (ii).
head: environment

label: con:P
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{con:P}
  We let 
  \[ \operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C}) \ = \ {\bigoplus}_{i\geq 0}\,\operatorname{Sym}^i(V_{\mathbb C}) \]
  denote the symmetric algebra of the complexification of an inner product space $V$.
  The value of the ultra-commutative monoid ${\mathbf P}$ at $V$ is then
  \[ {\mathbf P}(V)\ = \ P(\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C})) \ ,\]
  the complex projective space of the symmetric algebra.
  The structure map ${\mathbf P}(\varphi)\colon {\mathbf P}(V)\longrightarrow{\mathbf P}(W)$
  induced by a linear isometric embedding $\varphi\colon V\longrightarrow W$
  is given by  
  \[ {\mathbf P}(\varphi)(L) \ = \ \operatorname{Sym}(\varphi_{\mathbb C})(L)\ , \]
  where $\operatorname{Sym}(\varphi_{\mathbb C})\colon \operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C})\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sym}(W_{\mathbb C})$
  is the induced map of symmetric algebras.   
  The symmetric algebra $\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C})$ is a commutative ${\mathbb C}$-algebra without zero divisors.
  So the multiplication of $\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C})$ descends to a well-defined abelian monoid structure 
  \begin{align*}
     {\mathbf P}(V)\times {\mathbf P}(V) = P(\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C}))\times P(\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C}))\ &\longrightarrow \ P(\operatorname{Sym}(V_{\mathbb C})) ={\mathbf P}(V)\\
    ({\mathbb C}\!\cdot\! x,{\mathbb C}\!\cdot\! y)\qquad &\longmapsto \qquad {\mathbb C}\!\cdot\!x y
  \end{align*}
  on the projective space. The map ${\mathbf P}(\varphi)$
  associated to a linear isometric embedding $\varphi$
  is a monoid homomorphism, so ${\mathbf P}$ becomes a continuous functor
  from the linear isometries category to topological abelian monoids.
  As explained in \cite[Proposition 2.3.5]{schwede:global},
  this structure gives rise to an ultra-commutative multiplication on ${\mathbf P}$,
  whose $(V,W)$-component is the composite
  \[ \mu_{V,W}\ : \ {\mathbf P}(V)\times{\mathbf P}(W)\ \xrightarrow{{\mathbf P}(i_V)\times{\mathbf P}(i_W)} \
    {\mathbf P}(V\oplus W)\times{\mathbf P}(V\oplus W)\ \xrightarrow{\text{multiply}} \
    {\mathbf P}(V\oplus W)\ .  \]
  Here $i_V\colon V\longrightarrow V\oplus W$ and $i_W\colon W\longrightarrow V\oplus W$ are the direct summand embeddings.
  The multiplicative unit is the unique element of ${\mathbf P}(0)=P(\operatorname{Sym}(0))=\{{\mathbb C}\!\cdot\! 1\}$.
head: environment
name: The global ultra-commutative monoid $\bP$

label: con:pre-Bott
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{con:pre-Bott}  
  We let $\nu_1$ denote the tautological representation of $T=U(1)$
  on ${\mathbb C}$ by scalar multiplication.
  The cofiber sequence of based $T$-spaces
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:Tcof}
    T_+ \ \longrightarrow \ S^0 \ \xrightarrow{\ i \ } \ S^{\nu_1} 
  \end{equation}
  induces a long exact sequence in any $T$-equivariant cohomology theory;
  here $i\colon S^0\longrightarrow S^{\nu_1}$ is the inclusion of $T$-fixed points.
  For global spectra, the restriction homomorphism $\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}$
  is split by the inflation homomorphism 
  $p_T^*\colon\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_*^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  along the unique homomorphism $p_T\colon T\longrightarrow\{1\}$, see \eqref{eq:define_restriction}.
  So the long exact sequence splits off a short exact sequence:
  \[   \xymatrix@C=10mm{
      0\ar[r] & \pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{i^*} &
      \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}}&
      \pi_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r] & 0 }   \]
  The class $1=p_T^*(\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(e_T))$ is the multiplicative
  unit of the ring $\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$. Because $\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(1- e_T)=0$,
  there is a unique class, the first {\em pre-Bott class} $b_1\in \pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  such that
  \[     i^*(b_1)\ = \ 1- e_T\ \in \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ . \]
  For $m\geq 2$, we define the $m$-th pre-Bott class by transferring
  the $m$-th power operation of $b_1$ from $\Sigma_m\wr T$ to $U(m)$.
  To this end we identify $\Sigma_m\wr T$ with a maximal torus normalizer of $U(m)$
  via the preferred embedding
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:preferred_embed}
    \Sigma_m\wr T\ \longrightarrow \ U(m)    
  \end{equation}
  that embeds $T^m$ as diagonal matrices,
  and that sends elements of $\Sigma_m$ to the associated permutation matrices.
  The image of this embedding then consists of the {\em monomial matrices},
  i.e., those unitary matrices
  that have precisely one nonzero entry in every row and in every column.
  The {\em $m$-th pre-Bott class} is then defined as
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_preBott}
    b_m \ = \ \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(P^m(b_1))\ \in \ \pi_{\nu_m}^{U(m)}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}) \ .
  \end{equation}
  The power operation $P^m$ was defined in \eqref{eq:define_P^m}.
  The gradings work out because the restriction of the tautological $U(m)$-representation
  $\nu_m$ to $\Sigma_m\wr T$ is the representation $\nu_1^m$.
  For definiteness, we also set $b_0=1$ in $\pi_0^{\{1\}}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
head: environment
name: The pre-Bott classes

label: rk:b_1_unique
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rk:b_1_unique}
  Since $\eta\colon\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf{KU}}$ is a morphism of global spectra,
  it induces a commutative diagram of short exact sequences:
  \[ \xymatrix{
      0\ar[r] & \pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{i^*} \ar[d]_{\eta_*}&
      \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}}\ar[d]_{\eta_*}&
      \pi_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r] \ar[d]^{\eta_*}& 0   \\
      0\ar[r] & \pi_{\nu_1}^T({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r]_-{i^*} &
      \pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r]_-{\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}}&
      \pi_0({\mathbf{KU}})\ar[r] & 0     } \]
  The rings $\pi_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ and $\pi_0({\mathbf{KU}})$
  are both isomorphic to ${\mathbb Z}$, and the right vertical map is a ring homomorphism,
  and hence an isomorphism.
  Both the rings $\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ and $\pi_0^T({\mathbf{KU}})$
  are Laurent polynomial rings over ${\mathbb Z}$ in one variable,
  namely the stable tautological class $e_T$
  in the first case by \cite[Corollary 4.1.13]{schwede:global},
  and its image $\eta_*(e_T)=[\nu_1]$ in the second case.
  So also the middle vertical map is a ring isomorphism.
  The five lemma lets us conclude that the left vertical map is an isomorphism.
  We show in Remark \ref{rk:preBott2Bott} below that the map $\eta_*$
  takes the pre-Bott class $b_1$ to the $T$-equivariant Bott class $\beta_{T,\nu_1}$
  of the $T$-representation $\nu_1$.
  By injectivity, $b_1$ is the unique preimage of $\beta_{T,\nu_1}$.
head: environment
name: Uniqueness of $b_1$

label: prop:phi^m_on_b_1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:phi^m_on_b_1}
  For every $k\geq 1$, the relation
  \[ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(e_T)\ = \ e_T^k \]
  holds in the ring $\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$, and the relation
  \[ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(b_1)\ = \ (1+e_T+\dots+e_T^{k-1})\cdot b_1 \]
  holds in the group $\pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\phi^k\colon {\mathbf P}\longrightarrow{\mathbf P}$ is objectwise the $k$-th power map,
  its effect on $\pi_0^G({\mathbf P})$ is the $k$-th power map in the abelian monoid structure,
  for every compact Lie group $G$. In particular, the effect of $\phi^k$
  on the unstable tautological class $u_T \in \pi_0^T({\mathbf P})$ is given by
  \[ \phi^k_*(u_T)\ = \  u_T^k \ . \]
  The stabilization map $\sigma^T\colon \pi_0^T({\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  is multiplicative, and the stable tautological class $e_T=\sigma^T(u_T)$
  is the stabilization of $u_T$. So the first relation
  $(\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(e_T) =  e_T^k$ follows.

  The $T$-equivariant fixed point inclusion $i\colon S^0\longrightarrow S^{\nu_1}$
  induces a commutative square:
  \[ \xymatrix@C=12mm{
      \pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]^-{ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*}\ar[d]_{i^*} &
          \pi_{\nu_1}^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[d]^{i^*}\\
      \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[r]_-{(\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*} &
          \pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})
    }    \]
  We thus obtain the relation
  \begin{align*}
    i^*((\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(b_1)) \
    &= \ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(i^*(b_1)) \ = \ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(1-e_T) \ = \ 1-e_T^k\\
    &= \ (1+e_T+\dots+e_T^{k-1}) \cdot (1-e_T) \\
    &= \  (1+e_T+\dots+e_T^{k-1}) \cdot i^*(b_1) \\
    &= \ i^*( (1+e_T+\dots+e_T^{k-1})\cdot b_1) \ .
  \end{align*}
  The second relation then follows because the restriction map $i^*$ is injective.
head: environment

label: prop:double_coset
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:double_coset}
  For all $m,n\geq 1$, the following double coset
  formula holds:
  \[ \operatorname{res}^{U(m+n)}_{U(m,n)}\circ\operatorname{tr}^{U(m+n)}_{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T}\ = \
    \operatorname{tr}^{U(m,n)}_{(\Sigma_m\wr T)\times (\Sigma_n\wr T)}\circ
     \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T}_{(\Sigma_m\wr T)\times (\Sigma_n\wr T)}
   \]
head: environment

label: eq:coset2L_n
title: Proof
body_md:
We refer to \cite[IV Theorem 6.3]{lms} or \cite[Theorem 3.4.9]{schwede:global} for the general
  double coset formula for $\operatorname{res}^G_K\circ\operatorname{tr}_H^G$ for two closed subgroups $H$ and $K$
  of a compact Lie group $G$; we specialize it to the situation at hand.
  We write ${\mathcal L}_{m+n}$ for the space of sets $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$
  of $m+n$ pairwise orthogonal lines in ${\mathbb C}^{m+n}$.
  The tautological $U(m+n)$-action on ${\mathbb C}^{m+n}$ induces a transitive action on ${\mathcal L}_{m+n}$,
  and the stabilizer of the set of coordinate lines
  is the subgroup $\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T$, embedded into $U(m+n)$ by \eqref{eq:preferred_embed}.
  So the map
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:coset2L_n}
         U(m+n)/(\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T) \ \cong \ {\mathcal L}_{m+n}\ , \quad
    A\cdot(\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T)\ \longmapsto \ \{{\mathbb C}\cdot A\cdot e_1,\dots,{\mathbb C}\cdot A\cdot e_{m+n}\}
  \end{equation}
  that sends $A\cdot(\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T)$
  to the set of lines spanned by the columns of $A$
  is an equivariant homeomorphism.

  Now we let $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$ be any set of $m+n$ pairwise orthogonal lines in ${\mathbb C}^{m+n}$.
  We consider the special case where at least one line $L_i$
  is neither contained in ${\mathbb C}^m\oplus 0^n$ nor in $0^m\oplus {\mathbb C}^n$.
  We claim that then the intersection of the stabilizer of the set $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$
  with the center of $U(m,n)$ is 1-dimensional.
  The center $Z(U(m,n))$ of $U(m,n)$ consists of
  the matrices  $(\lambda E_m)\oplus (\mu E_n)$ for all $\lambda,\mu\in T$.
  Since some line $L_i$ is neither contained
  in ${\mathbb C}^m\oplus 0^n$ nor in $0^m\oplus {\mathbb C}^n$,
  it is not stabilized by the matrix $(\lambda E_m)\oplus (\mu E_n)$
  for any $\lambda,\mu\in T$ with $\lambda\ne \mu$.
  So the intersection of the stabilizer of $L_i$ with $Z(U(m,n))$ 
  equals the center of $U(m+n)$.
  Since any line is stabilized by the center of $U(m+n)$,
  also the intersection of the stabilizer of the tuple $(L_1,\dots,L_{m+n})$
  of lines with $Z(U(m,n))$ equals the center of $U(m+n)$,
  and is thus 1-dimensional.
  The stabilizer of the tuple $(L_1,\dots,L_{m+n})$
  has finite index in the stabilizer of the set $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$.
  So the intersection of the stabilizer of the set $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$
  with $Z(U(m,n))$ is also 1-dimensional, as claimed.


  For every compact Lie group $G$,
  the center $Z(G)$ of $G$ normalizes any given closed subgroup $H$,
  so the group $Z(G)/(H\cap Z(G))$ injects into the Weyl group $W_G H=(N_G H)/H$.
  The center of $G=U(m,n)$ is isomorphic to $T\times T$, and hence 2-dimensional.
  We take $H=\text{Stab}\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}\cap U(m,n)$
  as the intersection of the stabilizer of the set $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$
  with $U(m,n)$; the claim we just established says that $H\cap Z(U(m,n))$
  is 1-dimensional. So the group $Z(U(m,n))/(H\cap Z(U(m,n)))$
  is 1-dimensional, and the Weyl group of $\text{Stab}\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}\cap U(m,n)$
  inside $U(m,n)$ is infinite.
  This means that the $U(m,n)$-orbit of the set $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$
  does not contribute to the double coset formula.
  
  We conclude that all contributions to the double coset formula
  come from sets $\{L_1,\dots,L_{m+n}\}$ of pairwise orthogonal lines
  for which each line is either contained in ${\mathbb C}^m\oplus 0^n$ or in
  $0^m\oplus{\mathbb C}^n$. The group $U(m,n)$ acts transitively on these,
  so they only contribute the principal summand to the double coset formula.

label: con:pre-Bott_of_V
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{con:pre-Bott_of_V}  
  We let $V$ be a unitary representation of a compact Lie group $G$,
  of complex dimension $m$.
  We let $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow U(m)$ classify $V$, i.e., $V$ is isomorphic to $\alpha^*(\nu_m)$. 
  We let $\psi\colon V\cong\alpha^*(\nu_m)$ be a $G$-equivariant ${\mathbb C}$-linear isometry.
  We write $\psi^\flat\colon \pi_{\alpha^*(\nu_m)}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \pi_V^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  for the isomorphism given by precomposition with
  the equivariant homeomorphism $S^\psi\colon S^V\cong S^{\alpha^*(\nu_m)}$.
  The {\em pre-Bott class} of $V$ is
  \[  b_{G,V}\ = \ \psi^\flat(\alpha^*(b_m))\ \in \ \pi_V^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ .     \]
  We claim that the class $b_{G,V}$ is independent of the choice of the pair $(\alpha,\psi)$.
  Indeed, if $\bar\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow U(m)$ is another continuous homomorphism
  with $\bar\alpha^*(\nu_m)\cong V$,
  then $\bar\alpha=c_g\circ\alpha$ for some $g\in U(m)$.
  The group of equivariant self-isometries of a unitary representation
  is path connected.
  So if $\bar\psi\colon V\cong \bar\alpha^*(\nu_m)$ is an equivariant isometry,
  then the composite
  \[ V \ \xrightarrow[\cong]{\ \bar\psi\ }\ \bar\alpha^*(\nu_m)\ = \ \alpha^*(c_g^*(\nu_m))
    \ \xrightarrow[\cong]{\alpha^*(l_g)\ }\ \alpha^*(\nu_m) \]
  is homotopic to $\psi$ through $G$-equivariant isometries,
  where $l_g\colon c_g^*(\nu_m)\cong \nu_m$ denotes translation by the element $g$.
  Hence $(\alpha^*(l_g)\circ\bar\psi)^\flat=\psi^\flat$.
  Inner automorphisms act as the identity on representation-graded homotopy groups
  of a global spectrum $X$, in the sense that
  \[ c_g^*\ = \ l_g^\flat\ \colon \ \pi_{\nu_m}^{U(m)}(X)\ \xrightarrow{\ c_g^*\ } \  \pi_{c_g^*(\nu_m)}^{U(m)}(X)
  \ ,\]
  by the same kind of argument that proves \cite[Proposition 1.5.10]{schwede:global}.
  Hence
  \begin{align*}
    \bar\psi^\flat(\bar\alpha^*(b_m))\
    &= \  \bar\psi^\flat(\alpha^*(c_g^*(b_m))) \
    = \  \bar\psi^\flat(\alpha^*(l_g^\flat(b_m))) \\
    &= \  \bar\psi^\flat((\alpha^*(l_g))^\flat(\alpha^*(b_m)))\
    = \  (\alpha^*(l_g)\circ\bar\psi)^\flat(\alpha^*(b_m))
    \ = \ \psi^\flat(\alpha^*(b_m)) \ ,
  \end{align*}
  as claimed.
head: environment
name: Pre-Bott classes of unitary representations

label: thm:fix of pre-Bott
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:fix of pre-Bott}\ 
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
    \item For all $m,n\geq 1$, the relation
      \[ 
        \operatorname{res}^{U(m+n)}_{U(m,n)}(b_{m+n}) \ = \  b_m\times b_n
      \]
  holds in the group $\pi_{\nu_m\times\nu_n}^{U(m)\times U(n)}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  \item
    For all unitary representations $V$ and $W$ of a compact Lie group $G$,
    the relation $b_{G,V}\cdot b_{G,W}=b_{G,V\oplus W}$
    holds in $\pi_{V\oplus W}^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Multiplicativity of pre-Bott classes

label: eq:power_restriction
title: Proof
body_md:
(i) We need a property of the power operations \eqref{eq:define_P^m}
  that specializes to the `restriction relation' in the definition
  of a global power functor for $V=0$, compare \cite[Definition 5.1.6]{schwede:global}.
  The concatenation group monomorphism $+\colon \Sigma_m\times \Sigma_n \longrightarrow \Sigma_{m+n}$
  is defined by
  \[ (\sigma+\sigma')(i) \ = \ 
    \begin{cases}
      \ \sigma(i) & \text{ for $1\leq i\leq m$, and}\\
      \sigma'(i-m)+m & \text{ for $m+1\leq i\leq m+n$.}
    \end{cases}
  \]
  We embed a product of wreath products by the monomorphism
  \begin{align*}
    (\Sigma_m\wr G)\ \times\ (\Sigma_n\wr G)\hspace*{1.3cm}
    &\longrightarrow\quad \Sigma_{m+n}\wr G \\
    ((\sigma;\, g_1,\dots,g_m),\, (\sigma';\, g_{m+1},\dots,g_{m+n})) \
    &\longmapsto \ (\sigma+\sigma';\, g_1,\dots,g_{m+n})\ .
  \end{align*}
  Then for all $x\in \pi_V^G(R)$, the power operations satisfy the relation
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:power_restriction}
    \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr G}_{ (\Sigma_m\wr G)\ \times\ (\Sigma_n\wr G)}( P^{m+n}(x) )\ = \
    P^m(x)\times P^n(x)      
  \end{equation}
  in $\pi_{V^m\times V^n}^{(\Sigma_m\wr G)\times(\Sigma_n\wr G)}(R)$,
  exploiting that $ \operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr G}_{ (\Sigma_m\wr G)\ \times\ (\Sigma_n\wr G)}(V^{m+n})=V^m\times V^n$
  as representations of the group $(\Sigma_m\wr G)\times(\Sigma_n\wr G)$.
  This relation is proved by direct comparison of representatives.
  Thus
  \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{res}^{U(m+n)}_{U(m,n)}(b_{m+n}) \
    &= \   \operatorname{res}^{U(m+n)}_{U(m,n)}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T}^{U(m+n)}(P^{m+n}(b_1))) \\
    &= \ \operatorname{tr}_{(\Sigma_m\wr T)\times (\Sigma_n\wr T)}^{U(m,n)}(\operatorname{res}^{\Sigma_{m+n}\wr T}_{(\Sigma_m\wr T)\times (\Sigma_n\wr T)}(P^{m+n}(b_1))) \\
_{\eqref{eq:power_restriction}}  &= \ \operatorname{tr}_{(\Sigma_m\wr T)\times (\Sigma_n\wr T)}^{U(m,n)}(P^m(b_1)\times P^n(b_1)) \\
    &= \ \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_m\wr T}^{U(m)}(P^m(b_1)) \times
             \operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_n\wr T}^{U(n)}(P^n(b_1)) \ =\ b_m\times b_n \ .
  \end{align*}
  The second relation is the double coset formula of Proposition \ref{prop:double_coset}.
  
  (ii)
  We may assume that $V=\alpha^*(\nu_m)$ and $W=\beta^*(\nu_n)$ for continuous homomorphisms
  $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow U(m)$ and $\beta\colon G\longrightarrow U(n)$.
  Then $V\oplus W$ is the restriction of the tautological $U(m+n)$-representation $\nu_{m+n}$
  along the composite
  \[ G\ \xrightarrow{(\alpha,\beta)}\ U(m, n)\ \xrightarrow{\text{incl}} \ U(m+n)\ . \]
  Hence
  \begin{align*}
    b_{G,V}\cdot b_{G,W}
    &=     \alpha^*(b_m)\cdot \beta^*(b_n)  =  (\alpha,\beta)^*(b_m\times b_n)
    =  (\alpha,\beta)^*(\operatorname{res}^{U(m+n)}_{U(m,n)}(b_{m+n})) 
    =  b_{G,V\oplus W}\ .\qedhere
  \end{align*}
head: environment

label: prop:Phi_after_P^m
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Phi_after_P^m}
  Let $k\geq 2$.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item 
  The following diagram commutes for all $n\geq 0$:
  \[ \xymatrix@C=6mm{
      \pi_n(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})\ar[rrr]^-{P^k}\ar[d]_{(\Sigma^\infty_+ \phi^k)_*} &&&
      \pi_{({\mathbb R}^n)^k}^{\Sigma_k}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar[d]^-{\Phi^{\Sigma_k}} \\
      \pi_n(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ar@{=}[r] &
      \Phi_n^{\{1\}}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}) \ar[rr]_{p_{\Sigma_k}^*} &&
      \Phi^{\Sigma_k}_n(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})  } \]
\item
  The relation
  \[ \Phi^{\Sigma_k}(P^k(b_{\operatorname{cl}}))\ = \ k\cdot p_{\Sigma_k}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}}) \]
  holds in the group $\Phi^{\Sigma_k}_2(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i)
  The counterclockwise composite sends the class of
  a continuous map $f\colon S^{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^n}\longrightarrow S^V\wedge {\mathbf P}(V)_+=(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})(V)$
  to the class of the composite
  \[ S^{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^n}\ \xrightarrow{\ f\ }\ S^V\wedge{\mathbf P}(V)_+ \ \xrightarrow{S^V\wedge\phi^k(V)_+}\
    S^V\wedge{\mathbf P}(V)_+ \ ,\]
  supported in the colimit system \eqref{eq:define_geom_fix}
  for $\Phi^{\Sigma_k}_n(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$
  at the trivial $\Sigma_k$-representation $V$.
  We get another representative for the same class in $\Phi^{\Sigma_k}_n(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  by stabilizing this representative along the $\Sigma_k$-equivariant
  linear isometric embedding $\lambda_V\colon V\longrightarrow V^k$.
  By expansion of definitions, this stabilized representative
  features as the counterclockwise composite in the following diagram:
  \[ \xymatrix@C=10mm@R=6mm{
      S^{(V^k)^{\Sigma_k}\oplus{\mathbb R}^n}\ar[r]^-\cong \ar[d]_{(\lambda_V\oplus{\mathbb R}^n)^{-1}}^\cong &
       ((S^{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^n})^{\wedge k})^{\Sigma_k}\ar[r]^-{(f^{\wedge k})^{\Sigma_k}} &
       ((S^V\wedge {\mathbf P}(V)_+)^{\wedge k})^{\Sigma_k}\ar[d]^\cong\\
       S^{V\oplus{\mathbb R}^n}  \ar[d]_f\ar[ur]_{\quad x\mapsto(x\wedge\dots\wedge x)}
       && (S^{V^k}\wedge {\mathbf P}(V)^k_+)^{\Sigma_k}\ar[dd]^{(S^{V^k}\wedge(\mu_{V,\dots,V})_+)^{\Sigma_k}}\\
       S^V\wedge {\mathbf P}(V)_+ \ar[d]_{S^V\wedge \phi^k(V)_+}
       \ar[urr]_{\qquad v\wedge L\mapsto  (v\wedge\dots\wedge v)\wedge (L,\dots,L)}
       && \\
       S^V\wedge {\mathbf P}(V)_+\ar[rr]_-{S^{\lambda_V}\wedge {\mathbf P}(\lambda_V)_+} &&
       \left(S^{V^k}\wedge {\mathbf P}(V^k)_+\right)^{\Sigma_k} = ((\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})(V^k))^{\Sigma_k}\quad
    } \]
  The unnamed isomorphisms consist of shuffling of factors and instances of $\lambda_V$.
  The clockwise composite around the diagram sends the class of
  $f$ to the class of $\Phi^{\Sigma_k}(P^k[f])$,
  so the claim comes down to the commutativity of the outer diagram up to based homotopy.
  The proof of that homotopy commutativity has two ingredients:
  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
  \item
    a path in ${\mathbb R}_{>0}$ from $1/\sqrt{k}$ to 1 to eliminate the scaling factor
    that is needed to make $\lambda_V$ an isometry;
    this rescaling path is used in the upper left triangle and in the lower trapezoid;
  \item
    the homotopy commutativity of the following diagram of spaces:
    \[ \xymatrix@C=25mm{
        {\mathbf P}(V)\ar[d]_{\phi^k(V)}\ar[r]^-{\text{diag}} &
        ( {\mathbf P}(V)^k)^{\Sigma_k} \ar[d]^{(\mu_{V,\dots,V})^{\Sigma_k}}\\
        {\mathbf P}(V) \ar[r]_-{{\mathbf P}(\lambda_V)} &  {\mathbf P}(V^k)^{\Sigma_k}
      } \]
    We write  $i_1,\dots,i_k\colon V\longrightarrow V^k$ for the embeddings of the summands.
    The clockwise composite sends $L\in {\mathbf P}(V)$ to ${\mathbf P}(i_1)(L)\cdot\ldots\cdot {\mathbf P}(i_k)(L)$,
    whereas the counterclockwise composite sends it to ${\mathbf P}(\lambda_V)(L^k)=({\mathbf P}(\lambda_V)(L))^k$.
    We set $\theta=\arccos(1/\sqrt{k})$.
    For $1\leq j\leq k$, 
    we consider the path of linear isometries $H_j\colon [0,1]\longrightarrow {\mathbf L}(V,V^k)$
    from $i_j$ to $\lambda_V$ defined by
    \[ H_j(t)(v)\ = \ \cos(t\theta)\cdot (0,\dots,0,v,0,\dots,0)\ +\ \frac{\sin(t\theta)}{\sqrt{k-1}}\cdot (v,\dots,v,0,v,\dots,v)\ , \]
    with the distinguished entries in this formula occurring in the $j$-th coordinate.
    Then 
    \[ {\mathbf P}(V)\times [0,1]\ \longrightarrow \ {\mathbf P}(V^k)^{\Sigma_k}\ , \quad
    (L,t)\ \longmapsto \ {\mathbf P}(H_1(t))(L)\cdot\ldots\cdot {\mathbf P}(H_k(t))(L)\]
    is the desired homotopy for the above diagram.
  \end{enumerate}
  This concludes the proof that 
  $p_{\Sigma_k}^*((\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*[f])=\Phi^{\Sigma_k}(P^k[f])$.

  (ii) The restriction homomorphism $\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}\colon\pi_0^T(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \pi_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$ takes the stable tautological class $e_T$ to the multiplicative unit $1$.
  So
  \begin{align*}
    (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*( b_{\operatorname{cl}})\
    &= \ (\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*( \operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1))\
    = \      \operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}((\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(b_1))\\
    & = \ \operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}((1+e_T+\dots+e_T^{k-1})\cdot b_1) \
     = \ k\cdot \operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1)\ = \ k\cdot b_{\operatorname{cl}}\ . 
  \end{align*}
  The third equation is provided by Proposition \ref{prop:phi^m_on_b_1}.
  Since
  $\Phi^{\Sigma_k}(P^k(b_{\operatorname{cl}}))=p_{\Sigma_k}^*((\Sigma^\infty_+\phi^k)_*(b_{\operatorname{cl}}))$
  by part (i), this proves the claim.

label: eg:norm_does_not_match
title: Example
body_md:
\label{eg:norm_does_not_match}
  As we now explain, the pre-Bott classes are not compatible with power operations,
  in the sense that
  the class $P^m(b_{G,V})$ is typically different from the class $b_{\Sigma_m\wr G,V^m}$
  for $m\geq 2$ and $V\ne 0$.
  The classical pre-Bott class $b_{\operatorname{cl}}=\operatorname{res}^T_{\{1\}}(b_1)$ is also
  the pre-Bott class $b_{\{1\},{\mathbb C}}$ of the 1-dimensional representation
  of the trivial group.
  The $\Sigma_2$-representation ${\mathbb C}^2$ is isomorphic to $\sigma\oplus{\mathbb C}$,
  the sum of the sign and the trivial $\Sigma_2$-representation.
  So on the one hand,
  \[ 
    b_{\Sigma_2,{\mathbb C}^2}\
    = \ b_{\Sigma_2,\sigma\oplus{\mathbb C}} \ = \  b_{\Sigma_2,\sigma} \cdot b_{\Sigma_2,{\mathbb C}}\
    = \
    b_{\Sigma_2,\sigma}\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}}) \ . 
  \]
  Hence
  \[ \Phi^{\Sigma_2}(b_{\Sigma_2,{\mathbb C}^2}) \ = \ \Phi^{\Sigma_2}(b_{\Sigma_2,\sigma})\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}})\ =_{\eqref{eq:Phi^G_of_char}} \
    (1-\sigma^\sharp)\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}}) \ . \]
  On the other hand,
  \[ \Phi^{\Sigma_2}(P^2(b_{\{1\},{\mathbb C}}))\ = \ \Phi^{\Sigma_2}(P^2(b_{\operatorname{cl}}))\ = \ 2\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}})\ , \]
  by Proposition \ref{prop:Phi_after_P^m} (ii).
  Proposition \ref{prop:monomial_basis} (ii) below and the fact that $b_{\operatorname{cl}}\ne 0$
  show that $2\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}})\ne  (1-\sigma^\sharp)\cdot p_{\Sigma_2}^*(b_{\operatorname{cl}})$
  in $\Phi^{\Sigma_2}_2(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$. So also $P^2(b_{\{1\},{\mathbb C}})\ne b_{\Sigma_2,{\mathbb C}^2}$.
head: environment
name: Incompatibility with power operations

label: eq:i^*_of_b
title: Example
body_md:
Let $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow T$ be a nontrivial character of a compact Lie group $G$.
  Then the geometric fixed point homomorphism
  $\Phi^G\colon \pi^G_{\alpha}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\longrightarrow \Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  from \eqref{eq:geom_fix_map} factors as the composite
  \[ \pi^G_{\alpha}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\ i^* \ }\
    \pi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\Phi^G}\ \Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ , \]
  where $i\colon S^0\longrightarrow S^\alpha$ is the inclusion of $G$-fixed points. We record the relation
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:i^*_of_b}
    i^*(b_{G,\alpha})\ = \ i^*(\alpha^*(b_1))\ = \ \alpha^*(i^*(b_1))\
    = \ \alpha^*(1-e_T)\ = \ 1-\alpha^*(e_T)\ .
  \end{equation}
  Hence
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:Phi^G_of_char}
    \Phi^G(b_{G,\alpha})\ = \ \Phi^G(i^*(b_{G,\alpha}))\ = \
    1-\Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T))\ = \ 1 -\alpha^\sharp\ .
  \end{equation}
head: environment

label: eq:define_Psi
title: Construction
body_md:
We recall the construction of the transfer
  \[  \operatorname{tr}_H^G \ \colon \ \operatorname{Hom}(H,T)\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)\ , \]
  where $H$ is a finite index subgroup of a compact Lie group $G$.
  The construction uses a transversal of $H$ in $G$, i.e., an ordered $m$-tuple 
  $\bar g=(g_1,\dots,g_m)$ of elements in disjoint right $H$-orbits such that
  \[ G \ = \ {\bigcup}_{i=1}^m \ g_i H \ ,\]
  where $m=[G:H]$ is the index.  The wreath product $\Sigma_m\wr H$ acts freely and transitively 
  from the right on the set of all such transversals, by the formula
  \[ (g_1,\dots,g_m)\cdot (\sigma;\,h_1,\dots,h_m)\ = \ 
    (g_{\sigma(1)} h_1,\dots,g_{\sigma(m)}h_m)\ .  \]
  We obtain a continuous monomorphism 
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:define_Psi}
    \Psi_{\bar g}\ \colon\  G\ \longrightarrow\ \Sigma_m\wr H
  \end{equation}
  by requiring that
  \[  \gamma \cdot\bar g \ = \ \bar g\cdot\Psi_{\bar g}(\gamma)  \ .     \]
  In more detail: the image $\Psi_{\bar g}(\gamma)=(\sigma;\,h_1,\dots,h_m)$ is determined
  by the relations
  \[ \gamma\cdot g_i \ = \ g_{\sigma(i)}\cdot h_i \]
  for all $1\leq i\leq m$. The transfer of an $H$-character $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$
  is then defined as the composite
  \[  G \ \xrightarrow{\Psi_{\bar g}}\ \Sigma_m\wr H \ \xrightarrow{[m](\chi)}\ T \ . \]
  The resulting $G$-character $\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)$ is independent of the choice
  of $H$-transversal.
head: environment
name: Transfer

label: prop:monomial_basis
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:monomial_basis}
  Let $G$ be a compact Lie group.
  \begin{enumerate}[\em (i)]
  \item The map
    \[ \operatorname{Hom}(G,T) \ \longrightarrow \ \Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ , \quad
    \alpha \ \longmapsto \ \alpha^\sharp \ = \ \Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T)) \]
    is multiplicative, and its extension to a ring homomorphism
    \[ {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)] \ \longrightarrow \ \Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\]
    is an isomorphism of rings.
  \item The morphism of graded-commutative rings
    \[  {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)] \otimes \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})
      \ \longrightarrow \ \Phi_*^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ , \quad
      \alpha\otimes y\ \longmapsto \ \alpha^\sharp\cdot p_G^*(y)\]
    is an isomorphism.
  \item  Let $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow T$ be a  continuous homomorphism.
    Then for every  $m\geq 1$, the relation
    \[ P^m(\alpha^*(e_T))\ = \ ([m](\alpha))^*(e_T) \]
    holds in the ring $\pi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.
  \item  Let $H$ be a finite index subgroup of $G$,
    and let $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ be a nontrivial continuous homomorphism.
    Then the relation
    \[ \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{H,\chi})))\ = \ 1- \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp \]
    holds in the ring $\Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$,
    where $m=[G:H]$ and $\Psi_{\bar g}$ is the monomorphism \eqref{eq:define_Psi}
    based on some $H$-transversal $\bar g$ in $G$.
  \item Let $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow T$ be a nontrivial continuous homomorphism.
    Then for every  $m\geq 1$, the relation
    \[ \Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(P^m(b_{G,\alpha}))\ = \ 1- ([m](\alpha))^\sharp \]
    holds in the ring $\Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$.  
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) By \cite[Proposition 2.2.23]{schwede:global},
  the bijection \eqref{eq:Hom(G,T)}  is multiplicative in the sense that
  \[ \alpha^*(u_T)\cdot \beta^*(u_T)\ = \ (\alpha\cdot\beta)^*(u_T)\]
  in $\pi_0^G({\mathbf P})$, for all continuous homomorphisms $\alpha,\beta\colon G\longrightarrow T$.
  The stabilization map \cite[(3.3.12)]{schwede:global}
  is multiplicative and natural for restriction homomorphisms, and thus
  \begin{align*}
    \alpha^*(e_T)\cdot \beta^*(e_T)\
   &=_{\eqref{eq:define_e_T}}  \  \alpha^*(\sigma^T(u_T))\cdot \beta^*(\sigma^T(u_T))\
      = \  \sigma^G(\alpha^*(u_T)\cdot \beta^*(u_T))\\
    &= \  \sigma^G( (\alpha\cdot \beta)^*(u_T))\
      = \   (\alpha\cdot \beta)^*(\sigma^T(u_T))\
  =_{\eqref{eq:define_e_T}} \ (\alpha\cdot \beta)^*(e_T)\ .
  \end{align*}
  This relation and the multiplicativity of the geometric fixed point map
  yield
  \[ \alpha^\sharp\cdot\beta^\sharp\ =\ \Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T))\cdot \Phi^G(\beta^*(e_T))
    \ = \  \Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T)\cdot \beta^*(e_T))
    \ = \  \Phi^G( (\alpha\cdot \beta)^*(e_T))\ = \ (\alpha\cdot\beta)^\sharp\ . \]
  For every compact Lie group $G$ and every $G$-space $A$,
  the abelian group $\Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ A)$ is free, with a basis
  indexed by the set $\pi_0(A^G)$. More precisely, the composite
  \[  \pi_0(A^G)\ \xrightarrow{\sigma^G} \ \pi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ A)
    \ \xrightarrow{\Phi^G} \ \Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ A) \]
  of the stabilization map
  and the geometric fixed point map identifies $\pi_0(A^G)$ with a ${\mathbb Z}$-basis of
  $\Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ A)$. For the underlying $G$-space of the global space ${\mathbf P}$,
  we have $\pi_0({\mathbf P}^G)=\pi_0^G({\mathbf P})$, and   \eqref{eq:Hom(G,T)} identifies this set with
  $\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)$.
  Moreover,
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^G(\sigma^G(\alpha^*(u_T)))\ = \
    \Phi^G(\alpha^*(\sigma^T(u_T)))\ = \
    \Phi^G(\alpha^*(e_T))\ = \ \alpha^\sharp
  \end{align*}
  for every continuous homomorphism $\alpha\colon G\longrightarrow T$,
  and hence these classes form a ${\mathbb Z}$-basis of $\Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$.

  (ii) Part (i) shows that the graded ring
  $\Phi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\otimes \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$
  is a free module over $\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$ with basis the classes
  $\alpha^\sharp\otimes 1$ for all $\alpha\in \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)$.
  Suspension spectra and geometric fixed points commute, in the sense that the composite
  \[ \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}^G)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sigma^G\ } \ \pi_*^G(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P} )\ \xrightarrow{\Phi^G}
    \Phi_*^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}) \]
  of the stabilization map and the geometric fixed point map is an isomorphism. 
  The fixed point space ${\mathbf P}^G=P(\operatorname{Sym}({\mathcal U}_G^{\mathbb C}))^G$ is the space of $G$-invariant
  lines in a complete complex $G$-universe, and hence the disjoint union over all
  $\alpha\in \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)$ of copies of ${\mathbb C} P^\infty$.
  More precisely, choices of linear isometries
  $\alpha_\flat\colon {\mathbb C}^\infty\cong \operatorname{Hom}^G(\alpha,\operatorname{Sym}({\mathcal U}_G^{\mathbb C}))$
  to the $\alpha$-isotypical summands in the complete universe $\operatorname{Sym}({\mathcal U}_G^{\mathbb C})$
  assemble into a homeomorphism
  \[ \operatorname{Hom}(G,T)\times {\mathbb C} P^\infty\ \cong \ {\mathbf P}^G\ . \]
  Stable homotopy groups take disjoint unions to direct sums, so the induced map 
  \[ {\mathbb Z}[\operatorname{Hom}(G,T)]\otimes\pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \longrightarrow \ 
    \pi_*(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P}^G)\]
  is an isomorphism.

  (iii)
  Like for any ultra-commutative monoid, the stabilization maps
  $\sigma^G\colon\pi_0^G({\mathbf P})\longrightarrow\pi_0^G(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  send power operations in the global power monoid ${\underline \pi}_0({\mathbf P})$
  to power operations in the global power functor ${\underline \pi}_0(\Sigma^\infty_+ {\mathbf P})$,
  by direct inspection.
  We abbreviate
  \[ p_m=[m](\operatorname{Id}_T)\ \colon \ \Sigma_m\wr T \ \longrightarrow \ T \text{,\quad so that\quad}
    p_m(\sigma;\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m)\ = \ \lambda_1\cdot\ldots\cdot \lambda_m \ .  \]
  Then
    \begin{align*}
    P^m(\alpha^*(e_T))\
      &= \  (\Sigma_m\wr \alpha)^*(P^m(e_T))\\
    _{\eqref{eq:define_e_T}}   &= \  (\Sigma_m\wr \alpha)^*(P^m(\sigma^T(u_T)))\
      = \  (\Sigma_m\wr \alpha)^*(\sigma^{\Sigma_m\wr T}([m](u_T)))\\
      &= \  (\Sigma_m\wr \alpha)^*(\sigma^{\Sigma_m\wr T}(p_m^*(u_T)))\
      = \  (\Sigma_m\wr \alpha)^*( p_m^*(\sigma^T(u_T)))\\
   _{\eqref{eq:define_e_T}} &= \  (p_m\circ(\Sigma_m\wr \alpha))^*(e_T)\  = \  ([m](\alpha))^*(e_T) \ .
  \end{align*}
  
  (iv)
  We show first that for every ultra-commutative ring spectrum $R$,
  the composite
  $\Phi^G\circ\Psi_{\bar g}^*\circ P^m\colon \pi_0^H(R)\longrightarrow\Phi_0^G(R)$  is additive.
  Indeed, the composite
  \[ G \ \xrightarrow{\ \Psi_{\bar g}\ }\ \Sigma_m\wr H \ \xrightarrow{\text{proj}} \ \Sigma_m \]
  classifies the action of $G$ on $G/H$ by left translation.
  Since this action is transitive, the image of the composite is a transitive subgroup
  of $\Sigma_m$, and hence {\em not} subconjugate to $\Sigma_k\times \Sigma_{m-k}$
  for any $1\leq k\leq m-1$. Consequently, the image of $\Psi_{\bar g}\colon G\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr H$
  is not subconjugate to $(\Sigma_k\wr H)\times(\Sigma_{m-k}\wr H)$ for any $1\leq k\leq m-1$. 
  Thus the composite
  \[ \Phi^G\circ \Psi_{\bar g}^*\circ \operatorname{tr}_{(\Sigma_k\wr H)\times (\Sigma_{m-k}\wr H)}^{\Sigma_m\wr H}\]
  vanishes for $1\leq k\leq m-1$, by \cite[Proposition 3.4.2 (ii)]{schwede:global}.
  So the desired additivity follows:
  \begin{align*}
   \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(x+y)))\
    &= \ \sum_{k=0}^m \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(\operatorname{tr}_{(\Sigma_k\wr H)\times (\Sigma_{m-k}\wr H)}^{\Sigma_m\wr H}(P^k(x)\times P^{m-k}(y))))\\
    &=\ \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(x)))\ +\ \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(y)))\ .
  \end{align*}
  The first equation is the generic formula for a power operation on a sum in a global power
  functor, proved for ${\underline \pi}_0(R)$ in \cite[Theorem 5.1.11]{schwede:global}.

  Now we turn to $R=\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P}$.
  The class $\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{H,\chi}))$ has representation-grading $\Psi_{\bar g}^*(\chi^m)$.
  Since $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$ is nontrivial, the $G$-fixed points
  of $\Psi_{\bar g}^*(\chi^m)$ are also trivial. So the geometric fixed point homomorphism
  $\Phi^G\colon \pi^G_{\Psi_{\bar g}^*(\chi^m)}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\allowbreak\longrightarrow \Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})$
  factors as the composite
  \[ \pi^G_{\Psi_{\bar g}^*(\chi^m)}(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\ i^* \ }\
    \pi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ \xrightarrow{\Phi^G}\ \Phi^G_0(\Sigma^\infty_+{\mathbf P})\ . \]
  Altogether we can now conclude
  \begin{align*}    \Phi^G( \Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{H,\chi})))\
    &= \  \Phi^G(i^*(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{H,\chi}))))\\
   &= \  \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(i^*(b_{H,\chi}))))\\
_{\eqref{eq:i^*_of_b}}    &= \  \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(1-\chi^*(e_T))))\\
    &= \  1- \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(\chi^*(e_T))))\\
_{\text{(iii)}}    &= \  1- \Phi^G(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(([m](\chi))^*(e_T)))\\
   &= \  1- \Phi^G( (\operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi))^*(e_T))\
      = \  1- \operatorname{tr}_H^G(\chi)^\sharp\ .
    \end{align*}


  (v)
  We apply part (iv) to the ambient group $\Sigma_m\wr G$, its subgroup
  $H=G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)$ of index $m$, and with $\chi=\alpha\circ q$,
  for $q\colon G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)\longrightarrow G$ the projection to the first coordinate.
  We use the transversal $\bar g$ of $G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)$ in
  $\Sigma_m\wr G$ consisting of the elements $((1 i);1,\dots,1)$ for $1\leq i\leq m$.
  Then the associated monomorphism \eqref{eq:define_Psi} 
  \[ \Psi_{\bar g}\  \colon \ \Sigma_m\wr G \ \longrightarrow \ \Sigma_m \wr(G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)) \]
  is a section to the homomorphism
  $\Sigma_m\wr q\colon\Sigma_m \wr(G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G))\longrightarrow\Sigma_m\wr G$.
  So we obtain
  \begin{align*}
    \Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(P^m(b_{G,\alpha}))\
    &= \ \Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(\Psi_{\bar g}^*((\Sigma_m\wr q)^*(P^m(b_{G,\alpha}))))\\
    &= \ \Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m( q^*(b_{G,\alpha}))))\\
    &= \
      \Phi^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(\Psi_{\bar g}^*(P^m(b_{G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G) ,\alpha\circ q})))\\
   _{\text{(iv)}} &= \ 1- (\operatorname{tr}_{G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)}^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(\alpha\circ q))^\sharp
      \ = \ 1- ([m](\alpha))^\sharp \ .
  \end{align*}
  The final equation uses that
  $\operatorname{tr}_{G\times(\Sigma_{m-1}\wr G)}^{\Sigma_m\wr G}(\alpha\circ q)=[m](\alpha)$,
  see \cite[Proposition 2.2.30 (iv)]{schwede:global}.
head: environment

title: Construction
body_md:
We let $V$ be a unitary representation of a compact Lie group $G$.
  A {\em monomial datum} for $V$ is a pair $(H,\chi)$
  consisting of a finite index subgroup $H$ of $G$,
  and a continuous homomorphism $\chi\colon H\longrightarrow T$,
  such that $V$ is isomorphic to the induced representation $\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)$.
  For $g\in G$, let $^g H=g H g^{-1}$ be the conjugate subgroup,
  and let $c_g\colon {^g H}\longrightarrow H$ be the conjugation isomorphism defined by $c_g(h)=g^{-1}h g$.
  Then the $G$-representation $\operatorname{ind}_{^g H}^G(\chi\circ c_g)$ is isomorphic to $\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)$.
  So the group $G$ acts on the set of monomial data for $V$ by 
  \[ {^g(H,\chi)}\ = \ (^g H, \chi\circ c_g) \ .\]
  A {\em monomial structure} on $V$ is a $G$-orbit of monomial data.
  We write $\operatorname{mon}(V)$ for the set of monomial structures on $V$,
  and $[H,\chi]\in \operatorname{mon}(V)$ for the monomial structure represented
  by a monomial datum $(H,\chi)$.
head: environment
name: Monomial structures

title: Remark
body_md:
If $(H,\chi)$ is a monomial datum for $V$, then in particular, the following
  two properties must be satisfied:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Since $\dim(\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi))=[G:H]$,
    the index of $H$ in $G$ equals the dimension of $V$.
  \item Since the character $\chi$ is a summand in $\operatorname{res}^G_H(\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi))$,
    it is also a summand in $\operatorname{res}^G_H(V)$.
  \end{itemize}
  A compact Lie group $G$ has only finitely many subgroups of finite index,
  and $\operatorname{res}^G_H(V)$ has only finitely many non-zero isotypical summands.
  So $V$ has only finitely many monomial data.
  Hence also the set $\operatorname{mon}(V)$ of monomial structures is finite.
head: environment
name: Finiteness of $\mon(V)$

label: prop:unique_mon
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unique_mon}
  Let $V$ be a unitary representation of a compact Lie group $G$.
  Suppose that $G$ has a unique subgroup of index $\dim(V)$.
  Then $V$ has at most one monomial structure.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every monomial datum is supported on the unique subgroup $H$ of $G$
  of index $\dim(V)$.
  By uniqueness, the group $H$ is in particular normal in $G$,
  so if $(H,\chi)$ is a monomial datum, then 
  \[ \operatorname{res}^G_H(V)\ \cong \
    \operatorname{res}^G_H(\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi))\ \cong \ \bigoplus_{g H\in G/H}  \chi\circ c_g\ .\]
  So any other monomial datum equals $(H,\chi\circ c_g)$
  for some $g\in G$, and is thus conjugate to $(H,\chi)$.
head: environment

label: eg:inflate_mon
title: Example
body_md:
\label{eg:inflate_mon}
  We let $\epsilon\colon G\longrightarrow K$ be a continuous epimorphism of compact Lie groups.
  If $(L,\lambda)$ is a monomial datum for a $K$-representation $W$, then
  \[ \epsilon^*(W)\ \cong \ \epsilon^*(\operatorname{ind}_L^K(\lambda))\ \cong \
    \operatorname{ind}_H^G(\lambda\circ \epsilon|_H)\ , \]
  where $H=\epsilon^{-1}(L)$. So $(H,\lambda\circ\epsilon|_H)$ is a monomial datum
  for the inflated $G$-representation $\epsilon^*(W)$.
  We claim that the resulting {\em inflation map}
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:inflate_mon}
    \epsilon^* \ \colon \ \operatorname{mon}(W)\ \longrightarrow \ \operatorname{mon}(\epsilon^*(W))\ , \quad
    [L,\lambda]\ \longmapsto \ [\epsilon^{-1}(L),\lambda\circ \epsilon|_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)}]
  \end{equation}
  is bijective.
  For injectivity we let $(L,\lambda)$ and $(L',\lambda')$ be monomial data for $W$ 
  that become conjugate after inflation. So ${^g}(\epsilon^{-1}(L))=\epsilon^{-1}(L')$
  and $(\lambda\circ\epsilon|_{\epsilon^{-1}(L)})\circ c_g=\lambda'\circ\epsilon|_{{\epsilon^{-1}}(L')}$ for some $g\in G$.
  Then $k=\epsilon(g)$ satisfies ${^k}L=L'$
  and $\lambda\circ c_k=\lambda'$, and thus $[L,\lambda]=[L',\lambda']$.
  For surjectivity we let $(H,\chi)$ be a monomial datum for $\epsilon^*(W)$.
  Then the kernel $N=\ker(\epsilon)$ of the epimorphism acts trivially
  on $\epsilon^*(W)\cong\operatorname{ind}_H^G(\chi)$.
